doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Humphrey Lyttelton as Britain's most influential jazz figure
summary: Vacher praises Lyttelton's fifty-year band, radio, books and aristocratic background, with Shearing, Dankworth, Scott and Tracey.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Who in your estimation is the greatest, or most influential British jazz product?

It’s difficult to say isn’t it? Well for different reasons I guess, there’s no question Humphrey Lyttelton has made an extraordinary impact. Humph will be 80 this coming year. He’s had a band now for 50 years. Every British player of consequence has been in that band. Humph’s also been, he’s a Renaissance man, he’s presented a Monday night best of jazz radio program for 30 years. He’s written several excellent books, both an autobiography and of explanation of musical study. He’s an excellent trumpet player.

He’s composed probably a hundred or more original compositions. And he has probably the highest profile. He’s a most interesting character. He’s from a very privileged background. He’s an old Etonian, I mean Eton is our most prestigious public school, or you’d call it a private school. He comes from aristocratic stock and here was this extraordinary man who moved into a world of playing jazz music, which somehow was at odds with that kind of background. He was an officer of the guards during the war, which was also very prestigious, yet he became what he is still today, you know, an outstanding trumpeter and performer. So I’d give him huge marks. He did a lot to put jazz on the map, if you like, in Britain. Others again were Shearing obviously, Johnny Dankworth would be a very powerful contributor, and Ronnie Scott for sure. And there’s other very good individuals, but I’d be hard put to think of someone very much better than Humph. Stan Tracey, a wonderful piano player.
